primary_cause: Rate-sensitive bank selloff tied to collapsing yields and recession fears
secondary_factors: General de-risking of financials and concern over credit quality
store_description: USB's 4.4% drop looks mainly like a duration/rates move. The market was repricing bank earnings power lower as investors rushed into Treasuries and began betting the Fed could cut as early as March.

primary_cause: Fear that virus would hit cross-border payments and travel-linked spend
secondary_factors: Broad selloff in travel-exposed payment networks and general market panic
store_description: Visa fell 5.2% because investors were increasingly discounting a sharp slowdown in international transaction volume especially as travel restrictions widened and COVID cases surged outside China. That thesis was later borne out when Visa said cross-border travel spending deteriorated rapidly.

primary_cause: Rising concern about Honeywell's aerospace exposure. Singapore Airshow withdrawal
secondary_factors: Broader industrial and supply-chain risk from COVID. IATA warned 4.7% air travel decline $29.3B revenue hit
store_description: HON's 4.3% drop likely reflected a combination of direct disruption signals including its Singapore Airshow withdrawal and a fast-worsening outlook for airline and aircraft activity that threatened aftermarket and OEM demand for Honeywell aerospace products.

primary_cause: Broad enterprise software/tech de-risking on COVID growth fears
secondary_factors: Investors rotating out of cyclical IT spending names after Apple's warning
store_description: ORCL's 3.2% drop appears to have been a sympathy move inside the broader tech selloff rather than a discrete Oracle headline. Apple's Feb 17 revenue warning and the worsening global COVID picture made investors less willing to pay for IT-spend-sensitive names.

primary_cause: Financial-sector de-risking driven by lower rates and macro slowdown fears
secondary_factors: Pressure on dealmaking and capital-markets expectations. Goldman had warned Feb 20 about COVID complacency
store_description: GS's 3.1% decline looks like a macro repricing of financial conditions with falling yields weaker risk appetite and concern that trading/investment banking activity could soften if COVID hit growth.

primary_cause: COVID-driven semiconductor supply-chain and capex fears
secondary_factors: Read-through from Apple's Feb 17 warning and general tech hardware derisking
store_description: AMAT's 3.6% drop appears to reflect fear that Chinese factory disruptions would delay tool shipments and customer spending. The market was already extrapolating from Apple's warning to suppliers and upstream semiconductor equipment vendors.

primary_cause: Broad biotech/pharma risk-off selling
secondary_factors: No concrete near-term COVID treatment upside priced yet. Remdesivir swings came later in March/April
store_description: GILD's 3.8% decline looks more like market beta than an adverse company development. The big remdesivir-specific swings came later not in the February 22-25 window.

primary_cause: Fear of auto supply-chain disruption and weaker global vehicle demand. South Korea cases jumped to 833
secondary_factors: Hyundai had halted Korea output on parts shortages. Exposure to Asia and cyclical sensitivity
store_description: GM's 4.0% drop fits the market's reassessment of autos as a China/Korea supply-chain story. The South Korea outbreak and prior production halts at peers showed how quickly parts shortages could hit assembly even outside China.

primary_cause: Feb 17 revenue warning still dominant overhang. Would miss March-quarter guidance
secondary_factors: Continued global market panic. Reuters: analysts estimated China smartphone demand could fall by half in Q1
store_description: Even though the warning came a week earlier it was still the dominant Apple-specific overhang. Apple said it would miss prior guidance citing both constrained supply and lower Chinese demand and that remained the clearest company-level reason the stock fell another 3.4% on Feb 25.

primary_cause: Broad medical technology/healthcare risk-off move
secondary_factors: Fears that non-urgent procedures routine diagnostics and global supply chains could weaken
store_description: ABT's 4.1% drop does not line up with a discrete company event. It looks more like investors derisking diversified medtech names ahead of what later became very real pressure on routine testing and elective-procedure-linked businesses.

primary_cause: Broad selloff in IT services/consulting on fears clients would delay projects
secondary_factors: Recession risk and reduced corporate tech spending expectations. Later cut outlook in March
store_description: ACN's 3.6% fall appears to have been anticipatory rather than reactive to a fresh release. Investors were already discounting slower consulting demand and pushed the stock lower before Accenture formally reduced its 2020 growth outlook in March.

primary_cause: Semiconductor selloff tied to COVID supply-chain and end-demand fears
secondary_factors: Apple's warning increased concern about broader electronics ecosystem. High-beta
store_description: AMD's 3.2% drop looks like a sympathy move within semis. Investors extrapolated from Apple's warning and China manufacturing disruption to broader chip demand and supply risk even though AMD itself had not yet issued a fresh warning.

primary_cause: Broad healthcare/biotech risk-off trading
secondary_factors: General market liquidation and demand for cash/safety overwhelming stock-specific narratives
store_description: AMGN's 3.4% fall appears not to be tied to a fresh company event. No discrete Feb 22-25 Amgen announcement that plausibly explains the move better than the broad tape.

primary_cause: Supplier read-through from Apple's revenue warning. Apple = 20% of Broadcom FY2019 revenue
secondary_factors: Broader semiconductor and hardware selloff on COVID disruption fears
store_description: AVGO's 3.1% drop likely reflected the market revisiting Apple-related exposure. Reuters noted Apple represented 20% of Broadcom's fiscal 2019 revenue so Apple's supply-chain and demand warning made Broadcom an obvious sympathy casualty.

primary_cause: Fear of hit to travel-and-entertainment card spend
secondary_factors: Consumer credit concerns and general financials selloff
store_description: AXP's 5.7% drop was steeper than most banks because its revenue mix was more directly exposed to travel and discretionary spend both of which investors expected to contract sharply as flights were suspended and outbreak fears spread.

primary_cause: Worsening outlook for airline customers on top of pre-existing 737 MAX stress
secondary_factors: General industrial selloff and supply-chain concerns. IATA warned 4.7% passenger decline $29.3B revenue at risk
store_description: BA's 4.3% decline looks like a compounded hit. The market was already worried about Boeing because of the MAX and the sudden travel-demand shock threatened airline finances future aircraft orders and the overall aerospace supply chain.

primary_cause: Lower-rate/recession-fear hit to bank earnings expectations
secondary_factors: Credit-loss fears and general financial-sector liquidation
store_description: BAC's 5.0% drop was consistent with a classic bank trade unwind. Lower Treasury yields reduced expected net interest income while the market also began discounting weaker loan growth and rising credit costs if the outbreak broadened.

primary_cause: Financial-sector risk-off and rate pressure
secondary_factors: Weaker market levels and lower client activity expectations hurting fee-based asset-servicing businesses
store_description: BK's 3.6% drop appears macro-driven. Collapsing yields falling markets and lower expected asset values all threatened revenue streams tied to custody servicing and market activity.

primary_cause: Sudden repricing of global travel demand. Airlines suspending routes
secondary_factors: Broader consumer discretionary selloff. IATA projected 4.7% decline in airline passenger demand
store_description: BKNG's 3.7% decline was a straightforward travel-exposure move. As investors processed route suspensions and a projected decline in airline passenger demand online travel agencies were repriced lower on expected booking cancellations and weaker new reservations.

primary_cause: Asset-manager selloff as equity markets dropped and risk assets were de-risked
secondary_factors: Concern that AUM-linked fees and ETF flows would suffer in volatility shock
store_description: BLK's 4.2% decline was consistent with the business model. When markets fall fee-earning assets fall too and BlackRock later described vast de-risking from Feb 21 to quarter-end as coronavirus hammered risk appetite.
